extracted.intended_audience: general readers; film and media students, filmmakers and critics interested in the mockumentary genre
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive criteria for the mockumentary film/TV genre: what defines it, how it is presented, common techniques, purposes (satire/parody), medium-specific notes, improvisational practice, and ethical concerns. Useful for creators and analysts evaluating authenticity, style, and intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition — fictional events presented as a documentary
rubrics_metrics.description: A mockumentary (a portmanteau of mock and documentary) is a type of film or television programme depicting fictional events, but presented as a documentary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The core requirement is that the work depicts invented or fictional material while adopting documentary conventions and the rhetoric of factual reporting. Example: This Is Spinal Tap is repeatedly cited as a paradigmatic modern mockumentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose — analysis or satirical commentary
rubrics_metrics.description: Mockumentaries are often used to analyse or comment on current events and issues in a satirical way by using a fictional setting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or creating a mockumentary, assess how effectively the piece uses fictional scenarios to critique or illuminate real social/political/cultural issues. Examples: The Office (workplace satire), political mockumentaries like Bob Roberts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parody of documentary form
rubrics_metrics.description: Mockumentaries may be used to parody the documentary form itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the work lampoons documentary conventions (tone, narrator authority, archival presentation) and whether that parody contributes to humor, critique, or meta-commentary. Anti-pattern: parody that merely imitates documentary aesthetics without clear satirical purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation formats and tonal approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Mockumentaries are often presented as historical documentaries, with B roll and talking heads discussing past events, or as cinéma vérité pieces following people as they go through various events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the chosen presentation mode (historical/archival framing vs cinéma vérité observational style) and how it supports narrative, irony, or comedic beats. Examples: use of talking-head interviews vs fly-on-the-wall scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentary techniques and production devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of documentary techniques such as B roll, talking heads, archival film footage, voice-over narration, and editing actors into historical archive footage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These devices establish documentary verisimilitude; assess their authenticity, how convincingly they mimic factual reportage, and whether editing choices create comedic dissonance (e.g., Woody Allen edited into archival footage in Zelig). Overuse or clumsy pastiche can undermine credibility or humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvisation in performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Mockumentaries can be partly or wholly improvised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many successful mockumentaries (notably Christopher Guest's ensemble films and improv TV like Reno 911!) rely on improvisation to produce naturalistic, unpredictable comedic moments. Evaluate performers' ability to sustain character and documentary tone under improvisation; anti-patterns include improvisation that loses narrative focus or comedic timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre distinctions — comedic vs dramatic 'pseudo-documentary' forms
rubrics_metrics.description: While mockumentaries are comedic, pseudo-documentaries are their dramatic equivalents; they should not be confused with docudrama (dramatic techniques combined with documentary elements to depict real events) or docufiction (documentaries contaminated with fictional elements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When classifying or judging a work, distinguish whether the intent is comedic parody, dramatic realism, or a hybrid. Mislabeling can lead to misplaced expectations and misreadings of tone and ethical stance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium-specific terminology and formats (film vs television vs radio/animation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Strictly speaking, a mockumentary refers to films, while the term 'comedy verite' refers to TV series; the style has also been incorporated into animation and radio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize format-specific conventions: TV series may adopt serial character development and comedic-verite rhythms (e.g., The Office, Parks and Recreation), animation can apply mockumentary devices to non-live-action material (e.g., Surf's Up), and radio has its own precedents (e.g., People Like Us). Assess how medium alters pacing, audience expectations, and technical affordances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of real people or celebrities in fictionalized roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Mockumentaries sometimes use ensemble casts or celebrities performing fictional versions of themselves to blur lines between reality and fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the ethical and comedic effects of celebrities or real-life figures portraying fictionalized selves (e.g., Reboot Camp's cast playing versions of themselves, Borat's interaction with real people). Consider consent, exposure of non-actors, and whether the approach strengthens satire or veers into exploitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical considerations and audience deception
rubrics_metrics.description: Mockumentaries can provoke ethical concerns when audiences are tricked into believing the fiction is real; creators have faced criticism for deceiving viewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the production intentionally misleads publics and whether that deception is defensible artistically or harmful. Example: Peter Jackson's Forgotten Silver received criticism when its mockumentary status was revealed. Ethical evaluation should consider disclosure, potential harm, and cultural context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical and stylistic lineage — precedents and expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Mockumentaries draw on a lineage of earlier work (e.g., Buñuel, Orson Welles' War of the Worlds, April Fools' news pranks) and on documentary/verité traditions; knowledge of those precedents informs production and reception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating or critiquing a mockumentary, situate it within historical precedents and documentary traditions to judge originality and the degree of subversion. Explicit referencing or pastiche of well-known documentary texts (as in Documentary Now!) is a common creative choice.
